# Atomic structure and basis {.unnumbered #atomic-structure-and-basis}

## Ground-state basis {#ground-state-basis}

The solver uses the coupled ground-state basis

$$
|F,m\rangle,
\qquad F=I\pm\frac12,
$$

for alkali atoms with electronic ground angular momentum $J=1/2$. The selected quantization axis defines $m$ and the matrix representation of laboratory spin operators.

The steady population model retains the diagonal entries

$$
p_{Fm}=\langle F,m|\rho_0|F,m\rangle.
$$

The RF calculation adds selected ground-state coherences around this diagonal state.

## Optical transitions {#optical-transitions}

D1 and D2 excited states are constructed in the same hyperfine notation. Dipole matrix elements enforce the spherical selection rule

$$
\Delta m=q,\qquad q\in\{-1,0,+1\}.
$$

Transition strengths are calculated from angular-momentum coupling coefficients. Pressure shifts, Doppler broadening, natural width, and hyperfine offsets determine the complex spectral response at each laser frequency.

## Quantization and laboratory axes {#quantization-and-laboratory-axes}

Pump propagation, RF drive, static field, and detected observables are entered as laboratory axes. The solver transforms the associated spin and polarization operators into the local frame defined by the chosen quantization axis.

The population approximation is most consistent when the static magnetic field is parallel to that quantization axis. Transverse static-field mixing is not included in the steady population solve.

## Multipole interpretation {#atomic-multipoles}

Atomic orientation is the rank-1, vector part of the density matrix and is detected through vector optical polarizability. Atomic alignment is the rank-2, quadrupolar part and is detected through tensor optical polarizability. These connections are developed in [CBOR and LDOR](cbor-and-ldor.qmd).

## Atomic properties collision reference {#atomic-properties-collision-reference}

The Atomic properties page has its own isotope and temperature settings in the
sidebar. It reports the per-atom self-collision rates
$R_{\mathrm{SE}}=n_{\mathrm{sat}}\sigma_{\mathrm{SE}}\bar v_{\mathrm{rel}}$ and
$R_{\mathrm{ER,self}}=n_{\mathrm{sat}}\sigma_{\mathrm{SD}}\bar v_{\mathrm{rel}}$,
where $\bar v_{\mathrm{rel}}=\sqrt{16k_BT/(\pi m)}$. Rates are in inverse seconds,
densities in inverse cubic centimetres, cross sections in square centimetres,
and velocities in centimetres per second. No pair-counting factor of one half
or nuclear slowing-down factor is applied to these per-atom collision rates.
The self electron-randomization estimate includes binary spin destruction only.

The editable self cross-section defaults are element based: K uses
$10^{-18}$, Rb uses $1.6\times10^{-17}$, and Cs uses $2\times10^{-16}$ square
centimetres, from [Liu et al., Table 1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06434-2).
Isotopes share the element value. Na has no verified built-in self cross section
in this reference set; the rate remains unavailable until the user supplies one.

Buffer-gas pressures are fill pressures $P_f$ at $T_f=298.15$ K (25 °C). For a
sealed cell of fixed volume, $P(T)=P_fT/T_f$ and $n_g=P_f/(k_BT_f)$, with the
appropriate pressure and volume conversions. Thus
$R_{\mathrm{ER},g}=n_g\sigma_g\sqrt{8k_BT/(\pi\mu)}$, where $\mu$ is the
alkali-buffer reduced mass. With a fixed cross section the rate grows as
$\sqrt{T}$, since heating does not change the number density in this cell.

The optical estimates use $\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=\beta P(T)$ and
$\delta\nu=sP(T)$. This is a constant-coefficient approximation using the
existing MHz/Torr data. Neither an additional temperature law for optical
coefficients nor one for the editable collision cross sections is assumed.
The broadening column is the buffer-gas Lorentzian FWHM contribution, excluding
natural and Doppler broadening. Blank entries denote unavailable coefficients
or cross sections. These reference calculations do not change the independent
electron-randomization inputs on the ACC Magnetometer page.
